blocks.text: First-in, first-out means the earliest accepted item is removed before later accepted items. Rejected items do not enter the sequence. If pushes of one, two, and three succeed, then pops return one, two, and three. A fourth push rejected because of capacity must not appear in a later pop, even if its payload happened to be written into some temporary location.

blocks.text: Define the transition in terms of logical state. A successful push appends one value and increases size by one. A failed full push leaves both size and sequence unchanged. A successful pop returns the front value, removes exactly that value, and decreases size by one. An empty pop reports absence without changing state. These statements are simple enough to test after every generated operation.

blocks.text: A queue does not require moving all remaining elements after each pop. A vector with repeated erase(begin()) would preserve FIFO behavior but shift its remaining suffix. A ring buffer instead advances a front index, while a deque uses another representation supporting efficient endpoint operations. The abstract behavior and the physical mechanism should be chosen independently.

blocks.text: Application semantics determine whether retrying a rejected push is safe. If a producer retries the same event, its stable identifier can help prevent accidental duplication at a higher layer. The queue itself only knows whether it accepted this call’s integer. It does not implement exactly-once delivery, durable acknowledgement, or recovery after a process crash.

Once an item is popped, the queue no longer owns the pending obligation unless the application explicitly requeues or records it. A production work system may need acknowledgement and retry states beyond a simple FIFO. Recognizing that gap prevents a teaching container from being mistaken for a complete messaging service.

paragraphs: Enqueue adds a value after all currently queued values. Dequeue returns the oldest remaining value or reports an empty queue. The optional result distinguishes an empty queue from a legitimate stored zero.

For the ring queue, the invariant is 0 <= size <= capacity, with head identifying the oldest occupied logical position when size is positive. A full insertion returns false before any slot is modified. This lets the caller decide whether to retry, apply backpressure, or record a dropped sample; the container does not silently make that operational decision.

First-in, first-out means the earliest accepted item is removed before later accepted items. Rejected items do not enter the sequence. If pushes of one, two, and three succeed, then pops return one, two, and three. A fourth push rejected because of capacity must not appear in a later pop, even if its payload happened to be written into some temporary location.

topics.title: 6.1.2 Implementing Circular Buffers
topics.summary: A circular buffer maps logical position k to (head + k) % capacity. The next insertion position is (head + size) % capacity; removing advances head by one modulo capacity and decreases size. Keeping an explicit size distinguishes full and empty states even when index positions coincide.

blocks.text: With capacity four, push ten, twenty, and thirty, then pop ten and twenty. The head is now at physical slot two and size is one. Logical order is determined by head and size, not by printing the backing array from index zero.

blocks.text: A deque permits insertion at both ends. This makes it useful when the next item is sometimes urgent enough to go at the front while ordinary work joins the back, or when an algorithm must maintain a sliding window. The data structure provides the operations; the application must still define whether reordering priorities is allowed.

blocks.text: Do not call a deque a contiguous vector with extra methods. Standard deque supports random access but does not promise one contiguous allocation containing every element. An index can be efficient without implying that a pointer to the first element can be advanced through the entire logical sequence as a raw array. Representation assumptions must come from the container contract, not from similar-looking syntax.

blocks.text: For a sliding window, indices are often more useful than copied values. A monotonic deque for a window maximum stores candidate positions in decreasing-value order. New values remove weaker candidates from the back, while expired positions leave from the front. Each position can be inserted and removed at most once, producing a useful amortized argument. This is an application of deque operations, not a guarantee that every algorithm using a deque is linear.

When comparing it with the worked ring, include the same capacity rejection rule in the reference model. Otherwise the two structures implement different contracts and a failed push cannot be compared fairly.

Do not attempt to make it concurrent by marking counters volatile; volatile is not a substitute for synchronization.

topics.summary: The reference deque is allowed to contain at most eight entries, matching the ring’s capacity. Before a generated push, the test checks whether the reference has room.
